analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans legally import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other countries for personal use.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let Americans bring home lower-priced prescription drugs from abroad, never left the Senate committee it was referred to and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the government to write rules letting individuals bring prescription drugs into the United States in their luggage or by mail from countries like Canada, where the same medicines often cost far less. It also would have fixed problems in a 2000 importation law that had never taken effect: removing a built-in expiration date, stopping drug makers from punishing importers with pricing or labeling conditions, and forcing regulators to start writing the implementing rules. It was introduced by Senator Stabenow in January 2001 and never received a hearing or a vote; the Senate committee it went to took no action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay for their own prescription drugs, especially seniors and the uninsured, who could buy the same FDA-approved medicines in Canada and other countries where government programs have negotiated much lower prices. Patients with fixed incomes or chronic conditions would save the most, since they face the highest recurring drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write regulations permitting individuals to import covered prescription drugs for personal use in their baggage or by mail from countries including Canada, Australia, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and South Africa [S3].
It would have removed the sunset provision from the Medicine Equity and Drug Safety Act of 2000, so the importation law would not have automatically expired [S2].

It prohibits drug manufacturers from imposing conditions on importers about resale prices, and stops makers from conditioning access to labeling on anything but a fair fee for printing and shipping labels — closing a known loophole that let manufacturers block importation [S3].

It required the Secretary to begin writing implementing regulations within 30 days even before the final safety certification, addressing the fact that the 2000 law's certification requirement had been used to keep importation from ever starting [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose sales at U.S. prices as patients buy the same medicines abroad at lower foreign prices. Federal health agencies would bear the cost of writing importation rules, tracking records, and studying safety [S3].

drawbacks.text: Safety regulators have historically argued that drugs mailed from abroad are hard to verify, and the bill itself acknowledges the risk by requiring a Secretary certification that importation poses no appreciable additional risk to public health before it takes effect [S3].

The personal importation pathway applies only to individual purchases, so it would not have delivered savings automatically; patients would still have to arrange purchases abroad or by mail, and enforcement logistics at ports and in the mail stream could be burdensome for customs and FDA [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients paying U.S. retail prices, the potential savings are large and immediate, since identical drugs are often sold for a fraction of the price in countries with government-negotiated prices. The counterweight is safety: mail-order drugs are harder to inspect, which is why the bill ties implementation to a Secretary's health-safety certification and builds in a five-year study of the imports' safety and purity [S3]. On balance, the bill was structured to let patients reach lower prices while leaving regulators with tools to screen out dangerous products, though it would have depended heavily on agencies writing and enforcing careful rules.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Stabenow introduced S. 215 on January 30, 2001 [S1].
The bill had no cosponsors at any point [S4].
On the day of introduction, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died at the end of the 107th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers were better off, because the bill that would have let patients import cheaper foreign versions of their drugs never advanced. Americans paying full U.S. drug prices gained nothing from its failure.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.role: Senator from Michigan and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the record shows a single Democratic sponsor and no organized floor opposition — the outcome was determined by committee inaction rather than a recorded split.

industries.note: The bill would have let patients buy identical medicines at lower foreign prices, cutting into sales made at higher U.S. prices, and would have barred manufacturers from using pricing or labeling conditions to discourage importation [S3]. U.S. patients' access to cheaper drugs comes directly out of manufacturers' U.S. pricing power.

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and wholesale drug distributors
industries.note: Personal importation would have let some customers bypass domestic pharmacies for maintenance medications, but it applied only to personal-use quantities and did not create a commercial import channel [S3].
